chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali Majilawayh (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated from his uncle Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Abul-Hasan Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Raqqi, from Abdullah ibn Jabala, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, from al-Hasan ibn Abdullah, from his fathers, from his grandfather al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon them), who said:

A group of Jews came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), and their most knowledgeable among them asked him. Among what he asked him was that he said to him: 'For what reason were you named Muhammad, Ahmad, Abul-Qasim, Bearer of Glad Tidings, Warner, and Caller?' The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'As for Muhammad, indeed I am praised on earth. As for Ahmad, indeed I am praised in Heaven. As for Abul-Qasim, indeed Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He, will divide on the Day of Resurrection the division of the Fire, so whoever disbelieves in me from the first and the last will be in the Fire, and He will divide the division of Paradise, so whoever believes in me and acknowledges my Prophethood will be in Paradise. As for the Caller, indeed I call the people to the Religion of my Lord, Exalted and Glorious is He. As for the Warner, indeed I warn of the Fire to whoever disobeys me. As for the Bearer of Glad Tidings, indeed I give glad tidings of Paradise to whoever obeys me.'
ai.seo_question: What is the meaning behind the Prophet's names Muhammad, Ahmad, and Abul-Qasim according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Mani al-Akhbar* via the chain of the Imams, this hadith elucidates the divine wisdom behind the Prophet’s names, linking 'Muhammad' and 'Ahmad' to universal praise on earth and in the heavens respectively. It further interprets 'Abu al-Qasim' as a reference to the ultimate division of humanity into the Fire and Paradise, while defining his prophetic roles as Caller, Warner, and Bearer of Glad Tidings. This narration underscores the multifaceted nature of prophethood in Shia theology, balancing eschatological judgment with active da'wah.
